hypothesis.title: N+1 query amplification from per-product round-trips
hypothesis.explanation: The endpoint executes 1 category check + 1 product list + 2 queries per product (reviews + inventory). With ~40 products/category (schema: 2000 products / 50 categories), that's ~82 sequential database round-trips per request. Even at sub-millisecond per query, cumulative latency pushes p99 well above 50 ms. The baseline p50 ~58 ms already exceeds the p99 target, confirming the steady-state cost, not just tail noise.
supporting_evidence: catalog.py loops over products and awaits two queries per iteration
baseline p50 57-58 ms > target p99 50 ms
app CPU 66-69% suggests significant time in application logic / await points
missing_evidence: actual db.query span count and latency distribution per request

proposed_experiment.rationale: If N+1 is the driver, the http span latency will closely equal the sum of db.query latencies within a request, and the db.query count per request will be ~80+. If false, db.query count will be low (e.g., 2-3) and http span will exceed sum of db.query spans, pointing elsewhere.

predictions.observation: db.query span count per http request
sum of db.query p99_ms vs http GET p99_ms
predictions.if_supported: sum of per-query p99 ≈ http p99 (within 20%)
predictions.if_refuted: http p99 >> sum of db.query p99 (unaccounted latency)

events.message: pool_saturation: Connection pool saturation queuing queries

hypothesis.title: Connection pool saturation queuing queries
hypothesis.explanation: Pool max_size=20. At 94 req/s × ~82 queries/req ≈ 7,700 queries/s. If each query holds a connection for ~0.5 ms, that's ~3.85 concurrent connections average, but burstiness at p99 could exhaust the pool, forcing requests to wait for a free connection. This queuing delay would inflate tail latency without increasing per-query work.
supporting_evidence: high query volume implied by N+1 pattern
db CPU 57-63% suggests DB not saturated, but pool wait is client-side
contradicting_evidence: app CPU 66-69% (not blocked on I/O wait)
no errors or timeouts in baseline
missing_evidence: active connection count vs pool max

proposed_experiment.rationale: If pool saturation adds tail latency, db_activity will show active connections hitting POOL_MAX_SIZE (20) and wait events like 'ClientRead'/'ClientWrite' during queueing. If false, active connections will stay well below 20.

predictions.if_refuted: wait events dominated by query execution (e.g., 'CPU')

events.message: db_internal_contention: PostgreSQL internal contention (locks, WAL, buffer pool) at high query rate

hypothesis.title: PostgreSQL internal contention (locks, WAL, buffer pool) at high query rate
hypothesis.explanation: Even with low per-query work, 7,700+ simple queries/s can cause contention on shared structures (WAL, buffer mapping locks, proc array). This would manifest as increased per-query latency at p99, visible in db wait events, without pool exhaustion.
supporting_evidence: high query rate implied by code structure
db CPU 57-63% shows DB is active
contradicting_evidence: small data set (2000 products, ~30k reviews) fits in memory
simple indexed queries unlikely to contend heavily

proposed_experiment.rationale: If DB internal contention inflates tail latency, db.query p99_ms will be significantly higher than db.query p50_ms (high variance), and db_activity wait events will show lock/WAL waits (e.g., 'WALWriteLock', 'BufferMappingLock'). If false, db.query latency will be tight (p99/p50 < 2x) and wait events will be 'CPU' or 'ClientRead'.

single-join-query: Replace the N+1 query pattern with a single SQL query that joins products, pre-aggregated reviews, and inventory using LEFT JOINs and a GROUP BY subquery. The database performs all aggregation and joining in one round-trip.

candidate.name: single-join-query
candidate.strategy: Replace the N+1 query pattern with a single SQL query that joins products, pre-aggregated reviews, and inventory using LEFT JOINs and a GROUP BY subquery. The database performs all aggregation and joining in one round-trip.
candidate.expected_effect: Reduces database round-trips from ~82 per request to 2 (category check + single aggregated query). Expected p99 well below 50 ms because total DB time becomes ~1-2 ms instead of ~70 ms. Telemetry will show http span ≈ db.query span (single query).
candidate.risks: Single complex query may be harder for the planner to optimize; stale statistics could lead to a bad plan. The GROUP BY subquery on reviews materializes an intermediate result proportional to the reviews table size, which could grow. All eggs in one basket: a query plan regression affects the entire endpoint. Debugging individual data sources becomes harder because they are fused.

events.message: bulk-fetch-python-merge: Keep the logical separation of concerns but batch the per-product queries into two bulk queries using PostgreSQL's ANY(array) construct. Fetch all products for the category, then fetch aggregated reviews for all those product_ids in one query, then fetch all inventory for those product_ids in one query. Merge the three result sets in Python using dictionaries keyed by product_id.

candidate.name: bulk-fetch-python-merge
candidate.strategy: Keep the logical separation of concerns but batch the per-product queries into two bulk queries using PostgreSQL's ANY(array) construct. Fetch all products for the category, then fetch aggregated reviews for all those product_ids in one query, then fetch all inventory for those product_ids in one query. Merge the three result sets in Python using dictionaries keyed by product_id.
candidate.expected_effect: Reduces database round-trips from ~82 to 4 (category check, products, reviews, inventory). Total DB time drops to ~3-4 ms. The Python merge adds negligible CPU/memory overhead (maps of ~40 entries). Expected p99 well below 50 ms. Telemetry will show 3-4 db.query spans per request.
candidate.risks: Still uses 3-4 round-trips instead of 1, so latency is higher than the single-query approach (though still far below the SLO). The ANY($1) array grows with products per category; if a category ever has thousands of products, the array size could become a concern (PostgreSQL has a 1GB protocol limit, but planning time grows). Application logic is more complex: two maps to build and a merge loop, increasing surface area for bugs. Correctness depends on the merge preserving the ORDER BY name from the products query.

events.message: lateral-join-single-query: Use a single query with PostgreSQL LATERAL joins (correlated subqueries in the FROM clause) to fetch per-product review aggregates and inventory rows. This keeps the per-product logical structure in SQL but executes it as one query plan, allowing the planner to choose the best join strategy (hash join, nested loop, etc.) without application-side round-trips.

candidate.name: lateral-join-single-query
candidate.strategy: Use a single query with PostgreSQL LATERAL joins (correlated subqueries in the FROM clause) to fetch per-product review aggregates and inventory rows. This keeps the per-product logical structure in SQL but executes it as one query plan, allowing the planner to choose the best join strategy (hash join, nested loop, etc.) without application-side round-trips.
candidate.expected_effect: Reduces round-trips to 2 (category check + single query with LATERAL joins). The planner can optimize the correlated subqueries into efficient joins. Expected p99 well below 50 ms. Telemetry shows http span ≈ single db.query span. The query plan is visible in EXPLAIN for tuning.
candidate.risks: LATERAL joins are PostgreSQL-specific, reducing portability (though the service uses PostgreSQL). If the planner fails to decorrelate the subqueries, it may execute them once per product row — effectively the same N+1 pattern inside the server, which would not improve latency. This risk is mitigated by the fact that the subqueries are simple aggregates and point lookups on indexed columns, which PostgreSQL typically optimizes well. The pattern is less familiar to many engineers, increasing maintenance burden. The query is still monolithic: a plan regression affects the whole endpoint.
